Let $f\in \mathbb{Z}[x]$ be an irreducible polynomial of degree $k>2$ (and suppose that $k\neq 2^l$ for any $l\geq 1$) such that the leading coefficient of $f$ is positive.
Does the set of integers $n\geq 1$ for which $f(n)$ is $(k-1)$-power-free have positive density?
If $k>3$, and for all primes $p$ there exists $n$ such that $p^{k-2}\nmid f(n)$, then are there infinitely many $n$ for which $f(n)$ is $(k-2)$-power-free?
In particular, does\[n^4+2\]represent infinitely many squarefree numbers?
#978: [Er65b,p.219][Er81h,p.178]
number theory
Erdős [Er53] proved there are infinitely many $n$ for which $f(n)$ is $(k-1)$-power-free, except when $k=2^l$ and $2^{k-1}\mid f(n)$ for all $n$. This latter exception is possible, for example if\[f(x)=k!\left(\binom{x}{k}+1\right).\]Hooley [Ho67] settled the first question, in fact providing a precise asymptotic for the number of such $n\leq x$.
Heath-Brown [He06] proved the answer to the second question is yes when $k\geq 10$, and Browning [Br11] extended this to $k\geq 9$ (in fact establishing an asymptotic formula for the number of such $n$). (This is under the assumption that there does not exist a prime $p$ such that $p^{k-2}\mid f(n)$ for all $n$, which Erdős did not state explicitly, but is an obvious necessary condition, and is discussed explicitly in [He06] and [Br11].)
In [Er65b] Erdős mentions the question of whether $2^n\pm 1$ represents infinitely many $k$th power-free integers, or $n!\pm 1$, but that these are 'intractable at present'. (See also [936].)
Additional thanks to: Sarosh Adenwalla, Moritz Firsching, and Yongxi Lin

 The DeepMind prover agent has formally verified that the answer to the second part of the question is 'False' by constructing an explicit counterexample polynomial (assuming our formalisation) of the question is correct). 
The polynomial $f(X) = X^6 + 33X^5 + 21X^4 + 63X^3 + 18X^2 + 24X + 48$ satisfies all the hypotheses (irreducible, degree $> 3$, degree not a power of $2$, positive leading coefficient, no fixed $p^5$ divisor) yet $f(n)$ is never $4$-powerfree. Irreducibility follows from Eisenstein's criterion at $p = 3$, since $3$ divides all non-leading coefficients but $3^2 = 9 \nmid 48$, the constant coefficient. The key observation is that $f(X) \equiv X(X-1)(X-2)(X-3)(X-4)(X-5) \pmod{16}$, and the product of $6$ consecutive integers is always divisible by $6! = 720$, which is divisible by $16 = 2^4$. So $2^4 \mid f(n)$ for all $n$, meaning $f(n)$ is never $4$-powerfree - contradicting the conclusion that infinitely many values should be. The full formal proof in Lean 4 is available here).

 On looking at the literature, in most papers on the subject (e.g. Heath-Brown or Browning) when asking for $f(n)$ to take on infinitely many $r$th power-free values they assume the natural condition that, for all primes $p$, there exists at least one integer such that $p^r\nmid f(n)$.
For example in [Br11] Browning writes 'It is conjectured that this is the only obstruction to $f$ taking on infinitely many $r$-free values'. 
Although Erdős does not state this explicitly in [Er65b] or [Er81h] he was certainly aware of this obstruction, and he probably had it in mind - when he wrote about this problem he generally had specific polynomials like $n^4+2$ in mind.
I think the existence of irreducible polynomials of degree $6$ that fail this necessary criterion, as in your example, is well-known to people in the field.

 In [Er53], Erdos defined $l$-th power free to be "not divisible by any integral $l$-th power greater than 1" and also assumed that "the highest coefficient in $f(x)$ is positive". This definition of power free suggests that Erdos considered $f n$ as natural numbers/nonnegative integers (at least for large enough $n$), which suggests that the assumption that the highest coefficient in $f(x)$ needs to be positive is necessary. If we don't assume this, infinitely many values of $f(n)$ may be negative and then it does not make sense to talk about set with positive density. May we include this assumption in the problem statement?
I also suggests changing "Does the set of integers ..." to "Does the set of natural numbers ..."

 See [Er53].
There are polynomials, the presented example is $k! \binom xk+k!$ ($k$ needs to be even or it is reducible), that are a multiple of $2^{k-1}$ when $k=2^{\ell}$.
So a condition had to be imposed for the general case to ensure there are infinitely many examples which are $(k-1)$ power-free.
Nevertheless, one could say the density is zero otherwise. So no additional condition was necessary for the subquestion.
For the final question: this is an example where the expression may be square-free. (so there is no obvious reason ruling out that it can infinitely often square-free, as was the case with $x(x-1)(x-2)(x-3)+24$)
